result.title: Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents: Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games
result.summary: Weight-space programming (WSP) uses language models to construct neural network weights without training. We test whether known game mechanics can be compiled into compact agents that generalise to held-out levels, renderings and start states within a game family. Writers receive simulator source with held-out level data removed for 20 privately authored, unpublished ARC-AGI-3-style game families. With a fixed 57k-parameter recurrent architecture, the strongest writer reaches 56% held-out-level success with feedback, while the four main writers' Python players reach 97-100%. An exploratory free-architecture condition reaches 68-90%. Learning from support-level examples transfers much less well, but these learners lack the source information given to writers. Written networks have a program-like structure: 93% of parameters are zero, and 90% of the rest are small integers or powers of two. NumPy players under comparable computation caps reach 91%, versus the networks' 79%. Training the strongest writer's architectures from scratch yields about 1% success within our budget. Written fixed-network weights are fragile, and standard PPO removes most of their success. Prompts for noise robustness increase tolerance by about four orders of magnitude for two of three writers, but PPO makes larger updates and still removes most success. These results demonstrate rule-to-network compilation in this setting, while showing limited benefits over Python programs and no successful combination with the tested PPO fine-tuning.

AI.brief_summary: 论文在 20 个未公开的 ARC-AGI-3 风格游戏家族上测试「weight-space programming」：用语言模型直接依据模拟器源码写出 57k 参数循环网络的权重而无需训练，比较其对未见关卡、渲染与初始状态的泛化，并与 Python 程序玩家、从头训练及 PPO 微调对照。
AI.relevance_reason: 其「直接把规则编译进权重、训练反而摧毁已有能力」的现象，可供核查 LVR 中训练监督与贡献分配是否会破坏已有的推理结构；但任务与状态载体不是 VLM latent，迁移仅为线索。
